prompt: Which statement best separates an SLO from an SLA?

options.text: An SLO is measured by engineering's tools, while an SLA is measured by the customers' own monitoring
An SLA carries contractual consequences such as credits; an SLO is an internal target with none
An SLO covers availability only, while an SLA covers latency, durability and freshness too
An SLA is always the stricter number, so the team aims above it to keep the SLO safe

explanation: The SRE book's test is consequences: an SLA is a contract with credits or termination if missed; without consequences it is an SLO. Who measures it does not define it; SLAs are normally computed from the provider's own data. Either can cover any SLI, so the availability-only split is invented. The SLA is usually looser than the SLO, not stricter, so the team hears about trouble before it owes money.

prompt: How much full outage does a 99.95% SLO allow over a 30-day window?

options.text: 4.32 minutes
43.2 minutes
21.6 minutes
3.6 hours

explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes and the budget is 0.05%, so 43,200 × 0.0005 = 21.6 minutes. 4.32 minutes is the 99.99% budget. 43.2 minutes is 99.9%. 3.6 hours is 99.5%.

prompt: What share of the 30-day error budget did the incident spend?
scenario: An API serves a steady 1,000 requests a second with a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. A bad deploy fails 30% of requests for 20 minutes before rollback.

options.text: About 46%
About 14%
About 2%
About 0.03%

explanation: Bad requests: 1,000 × 1,200 s × 0.3 = 360,000. Budget: 0.1% of 2,592,000,000 = 2,592,000. 360,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 13.9%. Equivalently 20 min × 30% = 6 min of full outage out of 43.2. About 46% treats the 20 minutes as a full outage (20 / 43.2). About 2% is the fast-burn alert's threshold, not this incident. About 0.03% divides bad requests by all requests rather than by the budget.

prompt: Which are good SLIs for a request-driven checkout API? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fraction of valid checkout requests returning a non-5xx response at the load balancer
Fraction of valid checkout requests completed in under 400 ms at the load balancer
Average CPU utilisation across the checkout fleet over the last five minutes
Mean response time of checkout requests averaged across all servers each minute

explanation: Availability and threshold latency, both as good-over-valid ratios measured near the user, are the textbook request SLIs. CPU utilisation is a cause signal users never experience; checkout can fail at 20% CPU or be fine at 90%. A mean response time hides the slow tail, so most users can be fine while a tenth time out.

scenario: The team's latency SLO is 99% of requests under 300 ms. Their Prometheus histogram has buckets at 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 second. The SLI dashboard shows 99.4% using the 0.25 bucket.

options.text: Fine as it is: 0.25 is stricter than 0.3, so the real SLI can only be better than the dashboard
Interpolate between the 0.25 and 0.5 buckets with histogram_quantile, which is exact here
Switch to the 0.5 bucket so the dashboard number is never overstated during an incident
Add a 0.3 bucket boundary so the SLI counts exactly the requests faster than the SLO threshold

explanation: A threshold SLI needs a bucket boundary at the threshold, so add le=0.3. Using 0.25 is conservative, but it can show the SLO breached when it is not, which means false pages and wasted budget arguments. histogram_quantile interpolates linearly inside a bucket, which is an estimate, not exact. The 0.5 bucket counts 400 ms requests as good, overstating the SLI, the opposite of what option c claims.

prompt: At a 99.9% SLO, what error rate corresponds to a burn rate of 14.4?
explanation: Burn rate = error rate / (1 − SLO), so error rate = 14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44%. 0.0144% divides instead of multiplying. 14.4% would be a burn rate of 144. 0.144% is a burn rate of 1.44, slower than the slow-burn page.

prompt: Which alert from the workbook's recommended set fires first, and roughly when?
scenario: A release introduces a bug that fails 0.5% of requests, steadily, on a service with a 99.9% SLO over 30 days. Alerts: page at 14.4x over 1 h (5 min), page at 6x over 6 h (30 min), ticket at 1x over 3 days (6 h).

options.text: The 3-day ticket, after about 14 hours, with the budget gone in about 6 days
The 6-hour page, after about 6 hours, because 0.5% is five times the budget
The 1-hour page, within minutes, because any error rate above 0.1% pages
None of them, because a 0.5% error rate stays inside a 99.9% SLO

explanation: 0.5% is a burn rate of 5, below both paging thresholds (14.4 and 6). The 3-day average passes 0.1% after 0.1 / 0.5 × 72 h ≈ 14.4 h, and at 5× the 30-day budget lasts 6 days. The 6-hour page needs a burn rate of 6, not 5. The 1-hour page needs 14.4×, not any breach. And 0.5% errors is five times the allowed 0.1%, so it is very much outside the SLO.

prompt: Why does the workbook's fast-burn alert also require the 5-minute window to be over the threshold?

options.text: So the alert detects a total outage faster than the 1-hour window alone could manage
So the alert resolves within minutes of recovery instead of staying on for up to an hour
So that short spikes alone can page, since the 1-hour window by itself would smooth them out
So Prometheus evaluates fewer samples per rule and the query stays cheap to compute

explanation: The short window fixes reset time: after recovery the 1-hour average stays high, but the 5-minute one drops quickly, and both must be true to fire. Detection speed is set by the long window, because both must exceed the threshold; the short one never makes it fire earlier. Short spikes alone cannot page, since the 1-hour condition must also hold. The extra window adds a query, so it does not make evaluation cheaper.

scenario: Checkout calls payments, inventory and fraud in series. Each has a 99.9% SLO and they fail independently. Product asks checkout to commit to a 99.95% SLO.

options.text: Agree: checkout's own code is very stable, so hitting 99.95% only depends on the checkout team
Agree, if checkout's SLA is set at 99.95% too so that both numbers are equal
Decline: about 99.7% is the ceiling unless calls get retries, caching or redundant paths
Decline: an SLO can never be higher than the lowest single dependency's SLA

explanation: Serial independent dependencies multiply: 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%, so 99.95% is impossible without changing the design (retries for transient errors, caching inventory, a fallback payments provider). Checkout's own stability cannot beat its dependencies. Setting an equal SLA only adds financial penalties. The never-higher rule is too strong: redundancy can lift a service above any single dependency.

prompt: Under a typical error budget policy, what should happen next?
scenario: A service has spent 110% of its rolling 28-day error budget. A large feature launch is planned for Thursday. The policy freezes non-urgent releases while the budget is exhausted and names the VP of Engineering for disputes.

options.text: Launch anyway, since the budget resets automatically on the 1st of next month
Hold the launch and fix top budget consumers, or escalate to the named VP
Raise the error budget to 150% for this month so the launch can go ahead
Lower the SLO target quietly so the service is back within budget for now

explanation: The policy exists for exactly this: releases other than urgent fixes pause, the team works on what burned the budget, and anyone who disagrees uses the agreed escalation. A rolling 28-day window does not reset on the 1st; old bad days roll off gradually. Inflating the budget or quietly lowering the SLO during the crisis defeats the point of agreeing the numbers in advance; target changes belong in a planned review.

prompt: Which are sound reasons to prefer a request-based SLI over a time-based (good minutes) SLI for a busy API? Select all that apply.

options.text: A failure at peak traffic costs more budget than the same failure at 03:00
A 100% outage and a 2% error rate in one minute are no longer counted the same
It is always simpler to explain in a customer contract than counting minutes
It stays precise for services that only receive a handful of requests an hour

explanation: Request-based SLIs weight each failure by the users it hit, so peak failures cost more and partial failures cost less than total ones. Good-minutes SLIs are usually easier to put in a contract, which is why SLAs often use them. At a handful of requests an hour, one failure swings a request-based SLI wildly, so it is noisier, not more precise.
